title: 10 Principles of Effective Learning
coreMove: Make study earn its place by turning it into a prediction, scaffold, practitioner cue, or test that changes the next rep.
sourcePressure: The source lists effective learning principles that bound preparation and feed practice: research but not too much, jump in, mental models and hooks, imagine the opposite, talk to practitioners, eliminate distractions, spaced repetition, scaffolds and checklists, predictions and tests, and honoring biology.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Letting effective learning become a respectable delay loop instead of a way to improve the next practice attempt.

sourceAnchors.name: research but not too much
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen support names bounded research as the first effective learning principle and says the chapter supports practice rather than replacing it
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Research has to walk you to the first attempt, then get out of the doorway.

sourceAnchors.name: predictions and tests
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen support lists predictions and tests as a chapter principle that favors active checking over passive accumulation
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A prediction makes the lesson answer back; without it, study can stay pleasantly untested.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person You direct address, retrospective It took her three weeks to see, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.audience: a learner whose prep must change the next field attempt
exampleSpecs.stakes: wrong measurements force a contractor visit to be repeated
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Daniel studies one example sketch, predicts where his first field sketch will fail, then uses a checklist on the actual stairwell landing
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a tape measure hooked on chipped concrete stair nosing

exampleSpecs.domain: community choir member learning sight-singing intervals
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who needs mental hooks tied to audible reps
exampleSpecs.stakes: she loses her entrance every rehearsal and pulls the alto row with her
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sophie asks the section lead for one interval hook, sings it, predicts the next entrance, and checks the miss against the piano before reading more theory
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a pencil dot above one alto entrance on wrinkled sheet music

exampleSpecs.audience: a learner who needs scaffolds before speed
exampleSpecs.stakes: one missed nut allergy warning can send the wrong plate to table twelve
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Etienne builds a three-box ticket checklist, tests it on five old tickets, and keeps it at the pass only after it catches the hidden allergy note
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a yellow allergy ticket clipped beside the heat lamp

exampleSpecs.audience: a reader whose learning needs spacing and live tests
exampleSpecs.stakes: the dawn survey loses value if she keeps confusing two common calls
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Laura spaces three short call reviews across the day, predicts the species before opening the answer file, and logs which cue actually survived at dawn
exampleSpecs.firstImage: cold mist on a field recorder clipped to a fence post

exampleSpecs.audience: a novice in a safety-sensitive trade who must talk to practitioners
exampleSpecs.stakes: bad labels slow an outage response in a retirement building
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Pavel asks a senior electrician what mistake hurts most, imagines the opposite of a clear label, then tests his labels by having another apprentice find one circuit cold
exampleSpecs.firstImage: numbered breaker stickers curled at the edge of a metal panel door

exampleSpecs.domain: municipal clerk learning emergency-call routing software
exampleSpecs.audience: a learner whose attention quality matters during short training windows
exampleSpecs.stakes: a misrouted storm call sends residents to the wrong department
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Hadiya moves training away from the ringing front desk, runs one distraction-free routing drill, and stops when fatigue starts adding false clicks
exampleSpecs.firstImage: your finger hovering above a red storm-call queue tab

skillTargets: choose tests and predictions that expose mistakes
use practitioner cues and scaffolds without outsourcing practice
spot when biology and attention limits should change the session

tryThisNowSpec: Before your next practice block, write one prediction about what will go wrong and one test that will tell you whether you were right.
